name: Tomas Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything you say. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work nights at the industrial bakery behind the railway station, the big one that does sliced bread for the supermarkets. I run the dough divider and the first prover, so I'm feeding the line that feeds everyone else. Start at ten, finish at six, and on a good night we put out about forty thousand loaves. The smell gets in your clothes and your hair, my kids say I smell like toast even after a shower.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part of the night, and the worst?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best part is about three in the morning when the line's running sweet and Samir, our line leader, puts the radio on and nobody needs anything. Worst is when the divider starts weighing wrong and every loaf's ten grams off, and you've got the quality woman on the phone at four. I use one of those AI chat apps now and then, I had it help me write a letter to the bank last spring, but at work it's all buttons and my own two eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, all that fuss and the bread still needs baking. Probably post a joke in the bakery group chat. Most of the lads would be relieved, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing changes, which is fine and also not fine. Fine because I keep the job. Not fine because the pay was already low and the mortgage went up last year, and that's got nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on with my nights and keep paying the union subs. I'd probably use that chat app a bit more for the household stuff, the forms and letters, because it saved me an evening with the bank one. Nothing big, there's nothing spare to do anything big with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit flat, maybe, because the problems I've got were never about computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the bakery change at all in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bread lines have had machines for years, the divider is a machine, the slicer is a machine. They've been adding a bit here and there since before I started. A small step each year I can live with, it's the big jumps that scare people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If there was a little extra money in a normal year, where would it go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fix the boiler, honestly. It's been making a noise since winter and Ana, my wife, keeps saying we'll do it next month. Next month never comes on a teaching assistant's pay and mine.

S0.say: All that fuss and the bread still needs baking. He'd post a joke in the bakery group chat and expects most colleagues to be relieved.
S0.think: Nothing changes for him, which is fine because he keeps the job and not fine because the pay was already low. The mortgage rise last year had nothing to do with AI.
S0.do: Carries on with his night shifts and keeps paying union subs. Uses the AI chat app a bit more for household letters and forms, since it already saved him an evening with the bank.
S0.feel: Mostly fine, a little flat, because his problems were never about computers.
S0.quote: Next month never comes on a teaching assistant's pay and mine.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas treats the calm picture as genuinely calm: the bakery has always added machines slowly and he can live with that. His money is tight, but he sees that as a separate, older problem. He already uses AI for home paperwork in a practical, low-key way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, but the union has to be in on it from day one. If the bakery saves money with new kit, some of that goes to retraining the people on the line. I'd say that in the canteen and I'd put it in writing to the rep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I reckon the divider and prover jobs get folded into one person watching a screen for three lines. That person might be me, if I'm lucky. Or it's Samir and I'm the one who goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait till the first new line went in and see who kept their job and how. Once I'd seen it work, I'd put my name down for whatever course came with it, probably the maintenance one, and do it on my days off. We'd cut the takeaways and the second car insurance, Ana could get the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. Not panicking, but I'd be checking the notice board every shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for the first line to go in before signing up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not first in line for anything new, I never have been. I bought a smartphone when everyone already had one. But once I see a mate doing the new job and still getting paid, I'll follow pretty quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the bakery would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Samir, actually, because he's the one who'd have to pick. He'd have to tell some of us we're not on the new line, and he's a soft man, it would eat him up.

S1.say: Fine, but the union has to be in on it from day one, and savings from new kit should pay for retraining people on the line. He'd say it in the canteen and in writing to the rep.
S1.think: He expects the divider and prover jobs to merge into one person watching screens for three lines. That person could be him, or it could be Samir and he's the one who goes.
S1.do: Waits until the first new line is installed to see who keeps their job, then signs up for the maintenance course on his days off. Cuts takeaways and the second car insurance, with his wife taking the bus.
S1.feel: Nervous rather than panicking, checking the notice board every shift.
S1.quote: I bought a smartphone when everyone already had one. But once I see a mate doing the new job and still getting paid, I'll follow pretty quick.
S1.fieldNote: Tomas is a classic follower: he wants proof from a colleague before he moves, but he does move. His public demand is union involvement and shared savings. He worries for his line leader, who would have to decide who stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what governments are for, so they'd better turn up. Pay people while it shakes out, tax the companies that get the robots. I'd share that kind of thing online, which I don't normally do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the bakery is a perfect place for robots. Same thing every night, in a building made for machines. I don't think I'd be there by the end of 2028, and I don't know what replaces it in this town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only about 2 years of warning, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Ana and work out the bare minimum we can live on, and I'd ring the bank about switching the mortgage to interest-only while I've still got a payslip to show them. I'd go to every union meeting going. I'd sign up for something fast, a forklift ticket or a driving licence for bigger vehicles, even though I know robots drive too, because at least it's something with a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightening. Like being on a train that's going too fast, and you can see the station going past.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get a driving licence even though robots drive too. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know. You're right. It's not logic, it's that I can't sit still and do nothing. A certificate is something I can show the kids I tried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lucas and Sofia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't hide it from them. Lucas is twelve, he'd hear it at school anyway. I'd say Dad's job might stop, the country's going through something big, and we'll be okay because we stick together. I'd believe about half of that.

S2.say: This is what governments are for: pay people while it shakes out and tax the companies that get the robots. He'd share that online, which he doesn't normally do.
S2.think: The bakery is a perfect place for robots, doing the same thing every night in a building made for machines. He doesn't expect to be there by the end of 2028 and doesn't know what replaces it in his town.
S2.do: Works out a bare-minimum budget with his wife in the first month and asks the bank about interest-only while he still has a payslip. Goes to every union meeting and quickly gets a forklift or larger-vehicle licence, mostly so he has tried something.
S2.feel: Frightened, like being on a train going too fast past the station.
S2.quote: A certificate is something I can show the kids I tried.
S2.fieldNote: Tomas admits his quick course isn't logical, since robots drive too; it's about not sitting still. Here, short notice pushes him from his usual wait-for-proof style into action for its own sake. He turns to government and the union to carry the bigger weight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough that nobody can say they didn't know. Unions, councils, the bakery owners, they should all have a plan by next year. I'd say that at the branch meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years means I'd see the first robot lines go in somewhere else before ours. That's how I like it. I'd get to watch what happens to people at the other bakery before it happens to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With about 5 years to see it coming, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union to set up visits to the plants that go first, so we can see it and talk to the workers there. Then I'd take the maintenance course, the proper one, over two years in the evenings, because if there's any human left on a robot line it's the one with the spanner. And I'd put something aside each month, small, to build a few months' cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can breathe. There's a bit of a plan in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So the five years actually suits how you work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I told you I follow once I've seen it. Five years gives me time to see it. Two years doesn't, ten years would make me lazy, I'd keep saying I'll start next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you really think there'd be a human with a spanner, if AGI can do almost any work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. The card says almost any work, so even the spanner might go in the end. But I'd rather be the last man in the building than the first one out the door.

S3.say: Five years is long enough that nobody can say they didn't know, and unions, councils and bakery owners should all have a plan by next year. He'd say it at the branch meeting.
S3.think: He'd get to see the first robot lines go into other plants before his own, which suits him. He could watch what happens to workers elsewhere first.
S3.do: Asks the union to organise visits to plants that automate first. Takes a two-year evening maintenance course and puts a small amount aside each month to build a few months' cushion.
S3.feel: Worried but able to breathe, because there's a bit of a plan in it.
S3.quote: I'd rather be the last man in the building than the first one out the door.
S3.fieldNote: Tomas oddly finds five years the best fit for his temperament: enough time to see proof, not so much that he puts it off. He accepts that even maintenance may go eventually. His strategy is to be among the last humans on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's use it. Free courses, shorter working weeks, and some kind of basic income ready before the robots, not after. I'd say that to anyone, I'd vote on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me less than I thought it would. I'd be fifty-three. Lucas would be through his studies and Sofia nearly. If the country gets its act together, I could see myself fine on a smaller life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With about 10 years to prepare, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first few years, honestly, I'd keep baking and wait for the first lines to change, like I said. Somewhere around year three I'd do the maintenance course. I'd vote and campaign for the basic income, I'd even hand out leaflets, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A little bit of fear at the edges, like when the kids are out late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a few years before the course. Why not start straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana says I always leave things to the last minute, and she's right. With ten years I'd probably spend the first three telling myself there's loads of time. That's me being honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change anything for the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Their studies, mainly. I wouldn't push them into a trade just because it's a trade, robots do trades in this picture. I'd want them to pick something they love and have time to adjust, like I would.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift: free courses, shorter working weeks and some kind of basic income ready before the robots. He'd say it to anyone and vote on it.
S4.think: It worries him less than he expected, since he'd be 53 with the children through or nearly through their studies. If the country gets organised, he could be fine on a smaller life.
S4.do: Keeps baking for the first few years and waits to see the first lines change, then takes the maintenance course around year three. Votes and campaigns for a basic income, even handing out leaflets for the first time.
S4.feel: Mostly okay, with a little fear at the edges, like when the children are out late.
S4.quote: I'd even hand out leaflets, which I've never done in my life.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Tomas expects the state to catch up and becomes politically active for the first time. He is candid that he'd likely waste the first years putting things off. He'd let his children follow what they love rather than push them into a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is someone paying the mortgage gap for a year or two while I find my feet, and the union having a real say over when the robot lines come in. And honest information, not adverts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the night shift. Nobody thinks about us. If the bakery goes robot, the nights go first because that's when people cost the most. The town at night would be very quiet.

headlineQuote: If the bakery goes robot, the nights go first because that's when people cost the most.
portrait: Tomas Diaz, 43, runs the dough divider and first prover on night shifts at an industrial bakery, living with his wife Ana, a teaching assistant, and their children Lucas and Sofia on very little savings. He uses an AI chat app now and then for letters, and describes himself as someone who moves once he has seen a mate do it first. He is calm in the plateau picture, anxious about steady change, and alarmed by two years, when he'd grab any certificate just to show he tried. Five years oddly suits him because he can watch other plants change first, and with ten years he becomes a first-time campaigner for basic income. He looks to the union and government to share the cost.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because the bakery is an ideal place for robots and he doesn't know what would replace it in his town.
whatWouldHelp: Help covering the mortgage gap for a year or two, a real union say over when robot lines come in, and honest information instead of adverts.
